title: Det. No. 22-0048, 45 WTD 091 (2026)
description: An event-merchandise vending company (Taxpayer) protests an assessment by the Department of Revenue (Department). The Department’s assessment included adjustments for unpaid retail sales tax and service and other activities B&O tax. The Department also imposed an evasion penalty on Taxpayer for not remitting to the state the retail sales taxes it collected. Taxpayer contends that, as a consignee, it collected the retail sales tax on behalf of consignors, and it was not obligated to remit the retail sales tax to the state. Taxpayer failed to meet its burden to rebut the presumption that as the seller of tangible personal property it was required to collect and remit retail sales tax. As Taxpayer neither reported nor remitted the retail sales taxes it collected, the Department’s imposition of the evasion penalty was appropriate. However, some adjustments with respect to the assessment and in favor of Taxpayer, are warranted. We deny the petition in part and grant in part.

Det. No. 22-0048, 45 WTD 091 (June 9, 2026) 91
Cite as Det. No. 22-0048, 45 WTD 091 (2026)
BEFORE THE ADMINISTRATIVE REVIEW AND HEARINGS DIVISION
DEPARTMENT OF REVENUE
STATE OF WASHINGTON
In the Matter of the Petition for Correction of ) D E T E R M I N A T I O N
Assessment of )
) No. 22-0048
)
. . . ) Registration No. . . .

[1] WAC 458-20-159; RCW 82.04.480: B&O TAX – CONSIGNMENT –
AGENCY – CONTRACT TERMS. A contract for a consignment relationship that
designates the consignee as an independent contractor and makes no mention of a
principal-agent relationship will not satisfy WAC 458-20-159’s requirement that
the contract “clearly establishes the relationship of principal and agent.”
[2] WAC 458-20-159; RCW 82.04.480: B&O TAX – CONSIGNMENT –
REPORTING. When a consignee makes retail sales in its own name, those sales
are reportable under the retailing B&O tax classification and not the service and
other activities B&O tax classification. Likewise, credit card service fees to process
the retail transactions are reportable under the retailing B&O tax classification.
[3] WAC 458-20-228(5); RCW 82.32.090(7): EVASION – NOT
REPORTING OR REMITTING RETAIL SALES TAX COLLECTED. When a
taxpayer collects retail sales tax but does not remit it to the Department, and fails
to report it after backing it out in its own records, the taxpayer has demonstrated an
intent to evade under WAC 458-20-228(5).
Headnotes are provided as a convenience for the reader and are not in any way a part of the decision
or in any way to be used in construing or interpreting this Determination.
Willette, T.R.O. – An event-merchandise vending company (Taxpayer) protests an assessment by
the Department of Revenue (Department). The Department’s assessment included adjustments for
unpaid retail sales tax and service and other activities business and occupation (B&O) tax. The
Department also imposed an evasion penalty on Taxpayer for not remitting to the state the retail
sales taxes it collected. Taxpayer contends that, as a consignee, it collected the retail sales tax on
behalf of consignors, and it was not obligated to remit the retail sales tax to the state. Taxpayer
failed to meet its burden to rebut the presumption that as the seller of tangible personal property it
was required to collect and remit retail sales tax. As Taxpayer neither reported nor remitted the
retail sales taxes it collected, the Department’s imposition of the evasion penalty was appropriate.

Det. No. 22-0048, 45 WTD 091 (June 9, 2026) 92
However, some adjustments with respect to the assessment and in favor of Taxpayer, are
warranted. We deny the petition in part and grant in part.1
ISSUES
1. Whether, under RCW 82.04.480 and WAC 458-20-159 (Rule 159), Taxpayer met its burden
to demonstrate that it made sales as an agent and was thus relieved of its statutory duty to remit
retail sales tax it collected.
2. Whether, under RCW 82.04.290, the Department properly imposed the service and other
activities B&O [tax] on commissions and credit card fees.
3. Whether, under RCW 82.32.090(7) and WAC 458-20-228(5)(f) (Rule 228), the Department
properly imposed the evasion penalty.
FINDINGS OF FACT
Taxpayer sells merchandise and retail food items (collectively merchandise) at concerts and
various entertainment events. Third parties (Consignors) provide the merchandise, and generally
what is not sold is returned to the Consignors. At certain larger events, Taxpayer provides security
in addition to selling merchandise. It is not in dispute that Taxpayer collected retail sales tax on all
sales of merchandise that occurred from January 1, 2016, through June 30, 2019 (Audit Period).
The Department’s Audit Division discovered significant discrepancies between Taxpayer’s excise
tax filings and its bank statements for the Audit Period. Although Taxpayer made $. . . in deposits
during the Audit Period, Taxpayer only reported a total of $. . . in retail sales during the same.
Taxpayer’s excise tax returns did not reflect the actual deposits in the bank account because it did
not report the income and then take a consignment deduction, as it claims it is entitled to. Instead,
Audit Division determined that Taxpayer backed out the retail sales amounts in its records, thus
only reporting purported commissions from the retail sales. As such, although Taxpayer collected
$. . . in retail sales tax on the amount of gross sales verified by Audit Division, Taxpayer only
remitted $. . . in retail sales tax to the state. Audit Division assessed an outstanding balance of
retail sales tax due of $. . . .
At the outset of the audit, Taxpayer attempted to file amended returns and included a payment of
$. . . . The Department rejected the filings because the audit was ongoing. Because the amended
returns were not accepted, the Department applied the amount to the assessment liabilities.
Division Response at 5.
Audit Division also assessed the service and other activities B&O tax against portions of
Taxpayer’s income. Audit Division levied the service and other activities B&O [tax] against credit
card service fees collected by Taxpayer totaling $. . . for the Audit Period. Audit also levied the
service and other activities B&O tax against income Taxpayer received for providing security
while working certain events. The total unreported income for security was $. . . . Finally, Audit
1
Identifying details regarding the taxpayer and the assessment have been redacted pursuant to RCW 82.32.410.

Det. No. 22-0048, 45 WTD 091 (June 9, 2026) 93
Division determined that Taxpayer failed to report commissions, totaling $. . . , for consignment
sales made during the Audit Period.
Taxpayer asserts that the retail sales of merchandise were made on behalf of the Consignors. Some
of the Consignors, such as [Consignor 1], [Consignor 2], and [Consignor 3] are businesses that are
registered as making retail sales in the state. Some of the Consignors are artists and performers,
but Taxpayer does not provide evidence that any in this latter group of Consignors are registered
to do business in Washington or file excise tax returns. Also, Taxpayer did not provide receipts
from sales of merchandise made at events. Taxpayer asserted that the receipts from the credit card
sales made on behalf of [Consignor 1] indicated the sales were made in [Consignor 1]’s name.
Taxpayer, however, did not provide any receipts to verify this assertion.
Taxpayer states that the business relationship is informal with most of the Consignors and that a
principal/agency relationship is understood between the parties. Taxpayer provided a consignment
agreement with one Consignor, [Consignor 1] ([Consignor 1] Contract), to demonstrate the agency
relationship. The [Consignor 1] Contract states that Taxpayer is an independent contractor and
there is no employer or employee relationship for any purpose. [Consignor 1] Contract §12.
Additionally, Taxpayer agrees that [Consignor 1] will not be responsible for any claims arising
from Taxpayer’s performance of the contract. Id., §9. The contract does state, though, that
[Consignor 1] will be responsible for “attend[ing] to the administrative details of paying over to
the appropriate taxing authorities the sales taxes collected by [Taxpayer] and paid over to [
Consignor 1].” Id. §3(c). Also, Taxpayer must use the [Consignor 1] approved credit-card
machines. Id. §5. Nothing in the contract states that Taxpayer is the agent of [Consignor 1]. See
generally Id.
Taxpayer states that it did not collect all of the retail sales tax because two of the Consignors,
[Consignor 1] and [Consignor 2], own the credit card machines used by Taxpayer to make retail
sales at events. Taxpayer states that it does not have access to those funds because those payments
go directly to [Consignor 1] and [Consignor 2]. When sales at [Consignor 1] or [Consignor 2]
events are made in cash, Taxpayer collects the cash and deposits all proceeds into its own account.
Taxpayer collected all monies for sales, credit card and cash, made of merchandise it received
from [Consignor 3] and the various artists. Because Taxpayer essentially receives the merchandise
on credit, it then forwards payment for merchandise it sold to the Consignors after the events.
Taxpayer asserts that this amount includes the retail sales tax collected, and that those amounts are
then remitted by the Consignors to the state. Taxpayer did not provide receipts from any sales
made at events, so Audit Division could not confirm whether sales were made in the name of the
Consignors or Taxpayer.2
Audit Division reviewed Taxpayer’s books and records to account for the retail sales taxes
collected during the Audit Period. Audit was unable to reconcile Taxpayer’s books and records
with its assertions. Specifically, Taxpayer’s books and records lacked detailed accountings of retail
sales, retail sales tax collected, and commission if acting as an agent, so Audit Division could not
verify Taxpayer’s assertions that its payments to Consignors included retail sales taxes to then be
2 Taxpayer asserts that the receipts from sales made using [Consignor 1] credit card machines stated the sales were
made in [Consignor 1]’s name. Although offered an opportunity to provide such receipts following the hearing, it did
not.

Det. No. 22-0048, 45 WTD 091 (June 9, 2026) 94
paid by the Consignors to the Department. For example, Taxpayer’s records would show amount
totals for cash sales and credit card sales, but there were no data columns specifically addressing
retail sales tax, commission, or other incidental income. Although Taxpayer’s records reflected
payments to Consignors, those payments, which were made in one lump sum, were based on
calculations that were unclear to Audit.3 Thus, because Taxpayer did not keep its books and
records in a manner that was satisfactory to the Department, Audit Division assessed retail sales
tax on Taxpayer’s gross proceeds of sales during the Audit Period.
Audit Division also assessed the evasion penalty. In making its assessment, Audit Division stated
the following:
The auditor reconciled retail sales tax for the Audit Period. Your company did not
report any taxable retail sales for the first two quarters of 2016. In addition, for the
remaining Audit Period, you underreported taxable retailing income and retail sales
by an average amount of $. . . per quarter. . . .
Your prior company (a sole proprietorship) was previously audited by the
Department of Revenue for the period January 1, 2007, through December 31, 2010.
. . . During that audit, your company was assessed the 50 percent evasion penalty for
non-reporting income from the sales made at the . . . Arena in [City]. The previous
auditor explained in detail why your company was assessed the evasion penalty-
substantial underreporting of income.
The auditor reviewed historical reporting records from the Department of Revenue.
This current registration for your company was opened in January 2013. Your
company collected $. . . in sales tax during the Audit Period. Your company only
remitted $. . . of the collected sales tax. This is a net difference of $. . . that was not
remitted to the Department.
Audit Division Letter at 4-5. The evasion penalty totaled $. . . and was assessed against $. . . – the
$. . . unremitted retail sales tax and $. . . in service and other activities B&O tax.4
Taxpayer timely filed a petition for administrative review (Petition). Taxpayer’s argument against
the assessment on unreported retail sales tax is that the Consignors are deemed the sellers of the
merchandise and the Consignors file excise tax returns and remitted the sales tax collected by
Taxpayer to the Department. See, e.g., Petition at 6 (“Under RCW [82.08.040(2)(b)], [Consignor
1] is the seller of the merchandise, [Consignor 1] filed during the audit period Washington excise
tax returns, and remitted sales tax on its retail sales.”). Taxpayer asserts that it only acts as a service
provider and that the Department incorrectly included sales tax in Taxpayer’s assessment that the
Consignors remit. As such, Taxpayer protests “all adjustments and penalties except for use tax.”
Petition at 7. Taxpayer also asserts that it is a small business and unsophisticated in tax or financial
matters and that some of the recordkeeping duties were delegated to employees.
3 In briefing and at the hearing, Taxpayer’s representative attempted to clarify the bookkeeping deficiencies and
ambiguities.
4 The Department credited Taxpayer for retailing B&O [tax] that accounts for the difference. . . . Rounding
inconsistencies may be present.

Det. No. 22-0048, 45 WTD 091 (June 9, 2026) 95
Taxpayer asserts the five percent, substantial-underpayment penalty was improperly assessed. In
Taxpayer’s estimation, the Department miscalculated the amount of tax due by requiring it to remit
retail sales tax when, as it alleges, Consignors have also remitted the retail sales tax. Taxpayer
argues that it paid the proper amount due on its reported commissions, so there was no substantial
underpayment.
Taxpayer acknowledges that it kept inadequate recordkeeping and may not have contractual
agency agreements with Consignors. Taxpayer’s Third Response at 2 (stating its recordkeeping
was “weak”). However, Taxpayer takes a position that it need not formally comply with Rule 159
and agency can be deduced without a formal agreement and cites Det. No. 16-0243, 36 WTD 467
(2017), Det. No. 17-0147, 36 WTD 588 (2017), and Det No. 08-0301, 28 WTD 68 (2009) in
support of its argument. See Taxpayer’s Third Response. In support of its position that it had no
obligation to remit retail sales tax to the Department and that the Consignors instead remitted the
taxes collected, Taxpayer provided, among other things: copies of [Consignor 2]’s efiling
statements of its excise tax returns, Excel spreadsheets of sales from [Consignor 1] events to
demonstrate sales5, nine merchandise sales reports for [Consignor 1] consignments, settlement
reports, transaction reports indicating wire transfers to Consignors, accounting reconciliations
created by Taxpayer’s accounting representative, copies of processed checks from Taxpayer to
[Consignor 3], letters from [Consignor 1] and [Consignor 3] stating they filed excise tax returns
and paid retail sales taxes, and a summary of amounts of retail sales tax it asserts are due to the
Department.
Taxpayer’s argument against the evasion penalty is that the failure to remit the retail sales taxes
could not have been intentional because the Consignors were responsible for remitting and the
Consignors did in fact remit the retail sales taxes. Taxpayer asserts that the Department would be
collecting the retail sales tax twice if it were to also pay the taxes. However, Taxpayer
“acknowledges that it did not follow the procedures outlined in WAC 458-20-159[.]” Petition at
10. Even though Taxpayer had been audited for the same issue previously and knew it was
responsible for remitting the retail sales tax collected as consignee, Taxpayer stated it was merely
trying to comply with the business model required by Consignors. Taxpayer also alleges that
certain Consignors owned the credit card machines used to make the sales, and it never actually
had possession of those funds. Taxpayer states that, as set forth in Det. No. 92-133, 12 WTD 171
(1993), a prior imposition and payment of an evasion penalty does not establish a pattern of evasion
necessary to impose an evasion penalty in a subsequent audit. Petition at 11.
In its response to the Petition, Audit Division states that the amounts with regards to retail sales
tax collected by Taxpayer are not at issue. Additionally, at no time during the audit process, did
Taxpayer raise the issue that the Consignors had remitted the sales tax to the Department. Audit
Division’s position is that Taxpayer has not remitted the retail sales tax collected to the state nor
has it met its burden to show that the retail sales taxes were paid to the Consignors and then to the
state.
5 For example, the spreadsheets included the following data:
Item Total Return Sold Price Gross
. . . Black Youth Tee 68 44 24 $ . . . $ . . .

Det. No. 22-0048, 45 WTD 091 (June 9, 2026) 96
ANALYSIS
1. Seller and Seller’s Obligations
Washington imposes a retail sales tax on every retail sale of tangible personal property in the state.
RCW 82.08.020(1). “Sale” means any transfer of the ownership of, title to, or possession of
property for a valuable consideration. RCW 82.04.040(1). The term “retail sale” includes every
sale of tangible personal property, subject to certain exclusions, none of which apply here. RCW
82.04.050(1). Sellers must collect the full amount of the retail sales tax payable from buyers. RCW
82.08.050(1). If the seller fails to collect retail sales tax from the buyer or collects the tax and fails
to “pay it in the manner prescribed” to the Department, the seller becomes personally liable for the
amount of the tax whether the failure is the result of the seller’s actions or acts or conditions outside
of its control. RCW 82.08.050(3).
The term “seller” is a person “making sales at retail or retail sales to a buyer, purchaser, or
consumer, whether as agent, broker, or principal.” RCW 82.08.010(2). Here, Taxpayer asserts that
it is not responsible for remitting the retail sales tax because it is a consignee. Under Washington’s
tax code:
Every consignee, bailee, factor, or auctioneer having either actual or constructive
possession of personal property, or having possession of the documents of title thereto,
with power to sell such personal property in that person's own name and actually so
selling, is deemed the seller of such personal property within the meaning of this
chapter. Furthermore, the consignor, bailor, principal, or owner is deemed a seller of
such property to the consignee, bailee, factor, or auctioneer.
RCW 82.04.480(1) (emphasis added). When the consignee is deemed the seller, the consignee
“must collect and remit” the retail sales tax on each sale made. RCW 82.08.040(2)(a).
Taxpayer does not dispute that it had actual possession of the personal property with the power to
sell such personal property. Taxpayer argues that as a consignee it was not selling in its own name
but as an agent of the Consignors. However, under the Department’s administrative rule
implementing RCW 82.04.480, the “mere fact” that a consignee makes a sale “raises a
presumption” that the consignee sold in its name, and the “presumption is controlling unless
rebutted by proof satisfactory to the department of revenue.” Rule 159. Thus, “[t]he burden is on
the taxpayer in every case to establish the fact that the taxpayer is not engaged in the business of
making retail sales or wholesale sales but is acting merely as broker or agent in promoting sales
for a principal.” RCW 82.04.480(2); see Det. No. 08-0301, 28 WTD 68, 71 (2009) (“Sellers of
property are taxable on that activity unless they meet their statutory burden of proving that their
status was something other than that of seller.”). Accordingly, unless Taxpayer met the statutory
burden, Taxpayer was obligated to remit the taxes it collected to the state.
As a threshold matter, remittance to the state by consignors instead of the consignee is only allowed
when the consignor “is engaged in the business of selling tangible property” and the sale by the
consignee was made in the consignor’s name and the consignor “continues to be in business.” Rule
159. Taxpayer asserts that the Consignors, generally, are remitting the retail sales taxes. Taxpayer,

Det. No. 22-0048, 45 WTD 091 (June 9, 2026) 97
however, made sales on behalf of Consignors that were artists and performers, but Taxpayer
provided no information to demonstrate that traveling artists were or continued to be engaged in
the business of selling tangible property which would require them to file excise tax returns with
the state. Consequently, insofar as the Consignors were artists and performers, Taxpayer does not
meet its burden to show that the artists and performers may report and remit the retail sales tax
collected by Taxpayer.
We must then consider whether Taxpayer was acting as an agent for the Consignors who are in
the business of selling tangible personal property, [Consignor 1], [Consignor 2], and [Consignor
3], as demonstrated by their filing of excise tax returns and paying retail sales taxes. The
Department will allow an agency to claim when three circumstances are met. First, the taxpayer
must demonstrate that “the contract or agreement between such persons clearly establishes the
relationship of principal and agent.” Rule 159. Then, if a taxpayer has clearly established the
relationship of principal and agent, the taxpayer/agent must comply with two bookkeeping
requirements:
(1) The books and records of the broker or agent show the transactions were
made in the name and for the account of the principal, and show the name
of the actual owner of the property for whom the sale was made, or the
actual buyer for whom the purchase was made.
(2) The books and records show the amount of gross sales, the amount of
commissions and any other incidental income derived by the broker or
agent from such sales.
Rule 159 (emphasis added). Taxpayer’s claim that it was making sales merely as an agent of the
Consignors fails under each of the three requirements.
Taxpayer did not demonstrate that its agreements established an agency relationship
Taxpayer has not met its burden to show it had agreements with the Consignors that clearly
establish an agency relationship. Taxpayer states that it had informal relationships with most of
the Consignors, and the principal/agent relationship was understood by the parties. For the sales
on behalf of [Consignor 3], [Consignor 2], and the various artists and performers under which
there was no formal contract, Taxpayer has not “clearly established” a relationship of principal
and agent. See Rho Co. v. Dep’t of Revenue, 113 Wn.2d 561, 573, n.6, 782 P.2d 986 (1989)
(“Taxpayers who buy or sell tangible personal property on behalf of another will not be treated as
agents unless they have a contract expressly creating an agency relationship[.]”); Det. No. 16-
0243, 36 WTD 467, 478 (2017) (stating, for the purposes of Rule 159, substantiation must be made
through express language in written contracts).
Taxpayer provided the [Consignor 1] Contract to demonstrate its principal/agent relationship with
that Consignor. For the purposes of Rule 159, we may find an agency relationship has been created
when it is expressly stated in the contract. See Det. No. 16-0243, 36 WTD 467, 478 (2017). See,
e.g., Det. No. 08-0301, 28 WTD 68, 72-75 (2009) (determining an agency relationship did not
exist for the purposes of Rule 159 when not made explicit in the bylaws of a non-profit dairy

Det. No. 22-0048, 45 WTD 091 (June 9, 2026) 98
cooperative because the “Bylaws do not expressly use the term “agency” to classify the
relationship”). Although the [Consignor 1] Contract does not explicitly state that Taxpayer is the
agent of [Consignor 1] or [Consignor 1] is the principal of Taxpayer, terms in the agreement
indicate an agency relationship may exist. An agent principal relationship “results from the
manifestation of consent by one person that another shall act on his behalf and subject to his
control, with a correlative manifestation of consent by the other party to act on his behalf and
subject to his control.” Moss v. Vadman, 77 Wn.2d 396, 402-3, 463 P.2d 159 (1969). Consent and
control are the essential elements of agency. Id. at 403; see also Washington Imaging Services,
LLC. v. Dep’t of Revenue, 171 Wn.2d 548, 562, 252 P.3d 885 (2011). The relationship is created
by law, but if no facts exist to satisfy both elements of control and consent, “then no agency exists
despite the intent of either or both of the parties.” Moss, 77 Wn.2d at 403.
There are provisions of the [Consignor 1] Contract that indicate consent and control that may imply
agency. For example, the contract states that [Consignor 1] will attend to the details of paying the
retail sales taxes collected by Taxpayer, and [Consignor 1] agrees to use only [Consignor 1]
approved credit card machines. [Consignor 1] Contract §§ 3(c) and 5. Conversely, though, the
contract expressly states that Taxpayer is an independent contractor and [Consignor 1] would not
be responsible for any liabilities faced by Taxpayer as a result of performance of the contract. Id.
§§ 12 and 9. We find that the [Consignor 1] Contract does not offer clear evidence of the consent
and control necessary to find an agent/principal relationship. Taxpayer’s failure to keep its books
and records in accordance with Rule 159, discussed below, also leads us to this conclusion. Thus,
Taxpayer has failed to clearly establish that it was an agent of [Consignor 1] under the strict
requirements of Rule 159.6
As an agency relationship was not clearly established with any of the Consignors, it is not
necessary to determine whether Taxpayer met the bookkeeping requirements required of an agent
required by Rule 159. See Det. No. 16-0243, 36 WTD 467, 478 n.10 (2017). However, in this case,
we find it beneficial to address the bookkeeping requirements.
Bookkeeping Requirements
To comply with the first requirement, the books and records should demonstrate the transactions
were made in the name and for the account of the principal and show the name of the actual owner
of the property for whom the sale was made. The Department has previously determined that this
requirement is satisfied when the receipts indicate the sales are made on behalf of the
principal/consignor. See Det. No. 16-0243, 36 WTD 467, 478 n.10 (2017). Taxpayer did not
provide the Department with receipts that indicate the retail sales during the Audit Period were
made on behalf of the Consignors and not the Taxpayer. Taxpayer argues, however, that the fact
that two of the Consignors provided the credit card machines is proof that the sales were made on
behalf of the principals. Taxpayer’s argument only addresses who may have had access to the
funds and does not directly address the bookkeeping requirements. Additionally, a significant
portion of the retail sales during the Audit Period remain unaddressed by Taxpayer’s credit-card
machine argument. Taxpayer did not provide books and records to show the transactions were
6
. . . .

Det. No. 22-0048, 45 WTD 091 (June 9, 2026) 99
made in the name and for the account of the principal and show the name of the actual owner of
the property for whom the sale was made.
Likewise, Taxpayer’s books and records did not show the amount of gross sales, the amount of
commissions, and any other incidental income derived by Taxpayer from such sales to comply
with the second bookkeeping requirement. In fact, it was only during the administrative review
following the audit that Taxpayer’s accountant reconstructed the records to attempt to account for
the required information. Most or all of the clarifying spreadsheets and accompanying documents
were created in support of Taxpayer’s Petition by an accountant who did not work for Taxpayer
during the Audit Period. During the audit, Audit Division found that Taxpayer backed out the retail
sales tax, which resulted in the retail sales amounts not being reported on the excise tax returns
during the Audit Period. Consequently, we agree with the Audit Division that Taxpayer did not
keep books and records in accordance with the second bookkeeping requirement of Rule 159.
Taxpayer’s failure to meet the three requirements of Rule 159 means that Taxpayer did not
overcome the presumption in RCW 82.04.480(1) that it is by law the seller of the tangible personal
property. See RCW 82.04.480(2).
Unreported and Unremitted Sales Tax
When a seller collects retail sales tax from customers, the amount “is deemed to be held in trust
by the seller until paid to the department.” RCW 82.08.050(2). Furthermore:
if any seller, . . ., having collected the tax, fails to pay it to the department . . .,
whether the failure is the result of the seller’s own acts or the result or acts beyond
the seller’s control, the seller is, nevertheless, personally liable to the state for the
amount of the tax.
RCW 82.08.050(3). Sellers are specifically prohibited from appropriating or converting the tax
collected to the seller’s own use or to any other use other than remitting the tax to the Department.
In Kitsap-Mason Dairymen’s Ass’n v. Wash. Tax Comm’n, the Washington Supreme Court
explained the unique nature of the retail sales tax scheme and stated:
Inherent in RCW 82.08 is the fact that taxes collected in the name of the state are
not property of the seller. It is a misdemeanor to convert taxes collected to one’s
own use. The integrity of the entire taxing system demands that funds collected as
taxes be remitted to the state.
77 Wn.2d 812, 817, 467 P.2d 312 (1970). Taxpayer collected retail sales tax but appropriated the
funds for its own use by remitting the taxes to the Consignors. As such, we uphold Audit Division’s
assessment for unreported and unpaid retail sales tax during the Audit Period.7
7 Taxpayer made an argument against the substantial-underpayment penalty required by RCW 82.32.090(2) based on
its assertion that the Department incorrectly assessed retail sales tax. Having found the tax was properly assessed, it
is not necessary to address Taxpayer’s argument against the substantial-underpayment penalty. We do note, however,
that the tax assessed is corrected by this determination, and penalties will be calculated against corrected totals.

Det. No. 22-0048, 45 WTD 091 (June 9, 2026) 100
Additionally, as a seller making retail sales, Taxpayer’s gross proceeds of those sales are subject
to the retailing B&O tax. See RCW 82.04.250(1). Audit did not assess retailing B&O [tax], so an
adjustment will have to be made on the amount due . . . . See WAC 458-20-230(7)(a).
2. Service and Other Activities B&O Tax
Audit Division erred in imposition of service and other activities B&O tax on the purported
commissions. When a consignee does not prove an agency relationship, it should file excise tax
returns as follows:
• Report consignment sales under the Retailing B&O tax classification. You cannot
take a deduction for consignment sales.
• Report consignment sales under the Retail Sales tax classification.
• You do not have to report commissions on such sales.
Special Notice, Tax Reporting for Consignment Sales, issued July 2017 at 2; see also RCW
82.04.480(1); Rule 159. Here, the Consignors made a sale to Taxpayer, and Taxpayer made retail
sales in its own name. See RCW 82.04.480(1). Thus, there is no commission income to report. See
Det. No. 17-0147, 36 WTD 588, 590-91 (2017). As such, we cancel the portion of the audit that
assessed service and other activities tax against commissions.
For similar reasons, Audit Division’s imposition of the service tax on the credit card fees collected
is also in error. Retail sales tax is imposed on retail sales based on the selling price. RCW
82.08.020(1). “Selling price” is defined by RCW 82.08.010(1)(a)(i) to include, in relevant part:
[T]he total amount of consideration, . . . including cash, credit, property, and
services, for which tangible personal property [is sold] . . . whether received in
money or otherwise. No deduction from the total amount of consideration is
allowed for the following: (A) The seller's cost of the property sold; . . . (B) the cost
of materials used, labor or service cost, interest, losses, all costs of transportation
to the seller, all taxes imposed on the seller, and any other expense of the seller[.]
RCW 82.08.010(1)(a)(i).
WAC 458-20-108 (Rule 108) addresses “selling price,” and in the context of credit card service
fees, provides the following:
Credit card service fees. When a seller allows a buyer to charge purchases on a
credit card, the institution that issued the credit card charges a service fee to the
seller. The service fee charge is a part of the seller's cost of doing business. Because
the service fee is a cost of doing business, the seller may not deduct the fee when
determining its B&O tax and retail sales tax liabilities. RCW 82.04.070 and
82.08.010.
Rule 108(5). Because the fees are part of the selling price, they are subject to retail sales tax under
RCW 82.08.020 and retailing B&O tax under RCW 82.04.250. Thus, we cancel the portion of the
audit that assessed service and other activities B&O tax against credit card fees.

The service and other activities B&O tax should only be assessed against the $. . . for unreported
income received by Taxpayer for providing security. RCW 82.04.290(2)(a)(ii)(B).
3. Evasion Penalty
The Department also imposed the evasion penalty against the unpaid retail sales tax and unpaid
service and other activities B&O tax. A fifty percent penalty “must be” imposed when the
Department finds that “all or any part of the deficiency resulted from an intent to evade” a tax due.
RCW 82.32.090(7). The Department’s rule explains when the application of the penalty is
warranted:
The evasion penalty is imposed when a taxpayer knows a tax liability is due but
attempts to escape detection or payment of the tax liability through deceit, fraud, or
other intentional wrongdoing. An intent to evade does not exist where a deficiency
is the result of an honest mistake, miscommunication, or the lack of knowledge
regarding proper accounting methods. The department has the burden of showing
the existence of an intent to evade a tax liability through clear, cogent and
convincing evidence.
Rule 228(5)(f). As such, there are two elements to establish with clear, cogent, and convincing
evidence of an “intent to evade”: (1) knowledge of a tax liability and (2) an attempt to escape
detection or payment through deceit, fraud, or other intentional wrongdoing. Id.; Det. No. 13-0329,
33 WTD 156, 158 (2013). Clear, cogent, and convincing evidence has been described as evidence
convincing the trier of fact that the issue is “highly probable,” or, stated another way, the evidence
must be “clear, positive, and unequivocal.” Colonial Imports, Inc. v. Carlton Northwest, Inc., 121
Wn.2d 726, 735, 853 P.2d 913 (1993) (citation omitted).
There is clear and convincing evidence of Taxpayer’s knowledge of the tax liability. Business or
tax experience “tends to undercut or negate the possibility that a taxpayer was unaware that it was
required to report and pay taxes.” Det. No. 04-0098, 23 WTD 331, 338 (2004) (internal citation
omitted). Here, Taxpayer had business and tax experience, specifically a prior audit, that indicated
it was aware or should have been aware it must report and remit the retail sales taxes collected.
Taxpayer argues that there is not clear, cogent, or convincing evidence that it intentionally acted
to escape detection or payment. We first note that the intentional act could be to escape either
detection or payment. See Rule 228(5)(f). An intent to evade the tax exists when a taxpayer
willfully fails to remit to the Department the retail sales taxes collected from customers. Rule
228(5)(f)(ii)(B). It is undisputed that notwithstanding the prior audit, Taxpayer collected retail
sales tax and still did not remit to the state as obligated. Furthermore, Taxpayer’s excise tax filings
are proof of its willfulness to evade detection or payment of the tax. Although Taxpayer asserts
that it complied with the law because its intent was to report as a consignee making sales as an
agent, that argument is undercut by its filings and recordkeeping. In its audit findings, Audit
Division determined Taxpayer backed out retail sales, which obscured the tax liabilities on its
excise tax returns. Filing as an agent making consignment sales requires the following:

Det. No. 22-0048, 45 WTD 091 (June 9, 2026) 102
Report consignment sales under the Retailing B&O tax classification. A deduction may
then be taken when calculating the retailing B&O tax in the amount of the sales. The
deduction must be identified on the deduction detail as “Consignment Sales.”
Report consignment sales under the Retail Sales tax classification. Generally, the
Consignment Seller is responsible for remitting the sales tax to the Department.
(However, if the owner of the goods is registered with the Department of Revenue and
files excise tax returns, the seller can remit the sales tax to their customer to report to
the Department with their excise tax return. In this case, the seller can take a deduction
under “Other” then write in the explanation as “Sales tax remitted to owner.”)
Report commissions earned from consignment sales under the Service and Other
Activities B&O tax classification.
Special Notice, Tax Reporting for Consignment Sales, issued July 20178 at 1. Taxpayer did not
report the consignment sales under the Retailing B&O and then take its purportedly appropriate
deduction under consignment sales. Taxpayer did not report the consignment sales under the retail
sales tax classification and then take a deduction under Other, nor did it write an explanation of
sales tax remitted to owner/Consignors. Instead, Taxpayer backed out the retail sales in its own
records.
The law requires that taxpayer report the retail sales tax collected whether filing as the seller or
the agent. Thus, even under Taxpayer’s misguided argument that it was acting as an agent, it
willfully failed to report the collected retail sales taxes. In light of the Department’s published rule
that states failure to report and pay retail sales tax collected demonstrates an intent to evade, the
evidence demonstrates that the Department has met its burden to show knowledge of a tax liability
and the existence of an intent to evade detection or payment of the tax.
Once the Department has clearly established the elements of evasion, a burden of production is
imposed on the taxpayer to produce evidence of honest mistake, miscommunication, ignorance of
law, lack of knowledge, or some other fact that tends to rebut the Department’s evidence. Det. No.
16-0066, 35 WTD 540 (2016). Taxpayer argues that it was honest mistake which caused its failure
to remit the collected retail sales tax to the state. Taxpayer asserts its assumption that Consignors
would file excise tax returns and pay the retail sales tax it remitted to them alleviated its need to
remit the collected taxes to the state.
In 33 WTD 156, we upheld an evasion penalty when the taxpayer put forth a similar argument. In
that administrative review, the taxpayer argued that the mistake was that it filed in a manner similar
to a predecessor-in-interest. However, it was undisputed that, like here, the taxpayer knowingly
charged retail sales tax, willfully retained the amounts collected, and consciously did not report
them as taxes due when filing its excise tax returns. Id. at 159. Although the reason for the honest
mistake is different than in this case, the facts are similar in that Taxpayer collected the retail sales
tax, willfully refrained from remitting, and consciously did not report them as taxes due in its

rules and did not alter any taxpayer responsibilities. Additionally, Taxpayer had been made aware of its responsibility
for remitting the retail sales tax collected by a prior audit.

Det. No. 22-0048, 45 WTD 091 (June 9, 2026) 103
excise tax returns. And in that case, we determined that the Department met its burden of proof
with regards to the evasion penalty.
Finally, Taxpayer asserts that Det. No. 92-133, 12 WTD 171 (1993) stands for a Department policy
that payment of a prior evasion penalty does not prove evasion in a latter case. In 12 WTD 171,
there were two factors mitigating in the taxpayers’ favor that led us to cancel the evasion penalty.
First, the taxpayers sought advice from a tax attorney in their attempt at legal tax avoidance of
motor vehicle excise tax (MVET). Id. at 9. Second, because the . . . [taxpayers’] used the motor
vehicle at issue only sparingly in Washington, there was clear and cogent evidence that the
taxpayers may have been uncertain the MVET was due. Id. For those reasons, a prior evasion
penalty imposed on the taxpayer’s failure to pay MVET on a different motor vehicle was not
sufficient to again impose the evasion penalty. Id. Here, the mitigating factors are not present.
There is no evidence that Taxpayer conferred with tax professionals on how to lawfully comply
with Washington’s tax laws. It is also indisputable that Taxpayer was aware of its obligation to
report and also remit the retail sales taxes collected. As such, we find that 12 WTD 171 does not
provide a rationale for canceling the evasion penalty in this case.
Having considered Taxpayer’s evidence, we do not find that Taxpayer has demonstrated an honest
mistake, miscommunication, ignorance of law, lack of knowledge, or some other fact that tends to
rebut the Department’s evidence. Furthermore, the Department has routinely upheld the evasion
penalty where sales tax was collected but not remitted. See Det. No. 13-0329, 33 WTD 156, 159
(2013); Det. No. 14-0268, 33 WTD 637, 641 (2014); Det. No. 04-0098, 23 WTD 331, 339 (2004)
(“Any attempt to evade payment of collected retail sales tax is a serious matter.”).
Audit Division also imposed the evasion penalty against assessed service and other activities B&O
tax. However, there is not clear and cogent evidence of evasion of the tax due on providing
security, and we have cancelled assessment of the tax against commissions and credit card fees.
Thus, we uphold the imposition of the evasion penalty only as assessed against the unremitted
retail sales taxes collected but not remitted. See Rule 228(5)(f)(i) (stating the evasion penalty
applies only to the specific taxes that the taxpayer intended to evade).
DECISION AND DISPOSITION
Taxpayer’s petition is denied in part and granted in part.
